message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of tasks:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from operating systems to applications. | Specialized for parallel processing – originally built for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each very powerful with complex control logic, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores optimized for executing many identical operations simultaneously. |
| **Parallelism** | Mostly serial or limited parallelism; can handle a few threads at once. | Massive data‑level parallelism; can run thousands of lightweight threads concurrently. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory access, low latency. | Smaller per‑core caches, higher throughput memory, often uses dedicated VRAM. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Control flow heavy tasks, branching, I/O, single‑thread performance. | Data‑parallel workloads like matrix multiplication, image/video processing, deep‑learning inference/training. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set architecture (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC). | SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data) – same operation on many data points. |
| **Energy Efficiency** | Optimized for low power per core when doing general work. | Optimized for high throughput per watt for parallel tasks. |

In short, CPUs excel at tasks that require strong single‑thread performance and complex decision making, while GPUs shine when you need to perform the same operation on many pieces of data at once. This specialization makes GPUs ideal for graphics rendering, scientific simulations, and modern AI workloads.
